title: Pairing Across Centuries: Donne and Duffy

meta_desc: A-Level Comparative Poetry adventure pairing John Donne and Carol Ann Duffy across the centuries.
final_note: Donne and Duffy share more than they part on: dramatic speakers, witty rhetoric, the persistent argument with desire.

walkthroughs.body_html: Donne's 'The Flea' (Songs and Sonnets, published 1633 posthumously) is a seduction poem: a flea has bitten both lovers, mingling their blood, so they should mingle anyway. The conceit is exuberantly logical. Duffy's 'Mrs Aesop' (from The World's Wife, 1999) inverts: a wife's exasperated comic monologue dismantles her husband's pompous fables. Both poems are arguments-in-verse, addressed to a target. Comparison reveals Duffy's feminist reanimation of metaphysical address.

'The Flea' has three nine-line stanzas, each a stage of the argument: bite (stanza 1), defence against killing (stanza 2), pivot to seduction (stanza 3). 'Mrs Aesop' uses irregular stanzas of varied length, mirroring conversational impatience. Form mirrors argumentative shape: Donne's tight stanzas perform logical procession; Duffy's looser shape performs interruption. Both poems demonstrate that form is rhetorical.

Donne's speaker is a confident, witty male lover. Duffy's speaker is a sardonic wife. Both deploy second-person address as weapon — 'Mark but this flea' / 'By Christ, he could bore for Purgatory'. The comparative essay should track how address works: Donne uses imperatives to draw the addressee in; Duffy uses third-person narration to expose her husband to an implied audience while ostensibly speaking to him. Both invert the lyric tradition of solitary address.
